Phase 1 – Crawl: Setting the standards
The first phase for the platform team's success would be to define the standards for data
normalization across the company. This was a place where the observability team had
expertise, and they recommended the CDEvents specification, which is already an emerging
standard within idx_6c1aaa04 Kubernetes (https://cdevents.dev/). The mission statement on the home
page of the specification spoke exactly to the problems ACME Financial Services needed to
solve, and on top of the specification and adoption by some of the tools already used within the
company, CDEvents provides an SDK for several different programming languages to help
teams implement the specification. This would make it easier for application teams to make
the required changes to follow the new data standards. The team was able to tie this back to
the scaling opportunities the SRE team had highlighted, and they also noted it could help
reduce the time to produce RCA.
Here, the observability team was prioritizing the SRE team users, as that was the quickest
implementation with more immediate and measurable returns on investment.
The application teams benefited as well. The SRE team would be able to do a better job
supporting their applications, and they were already well-positioned for the platform adoption
that came in Phase 2.
Phase 2 – Walk: IDP with its first golden paths
Phase 2 was not wholly dependent on the completion of Phase 1. Both could be run in parallel.
The second phase was idx_28a0ad5f where the real work would begin for the new platform team. They
needed to meet with application teams and determine what the most common workflows
were that the platform could consolidate. Once they had identified one or two use cases, this
was where they would produce the thinnest viable platform (TVP). The TVP idx_51ccfed0 had two key
focus areas:
Helping application teams repeatably deploy their applications while meeting the
standards for metrics, as well as other standardized steps for building and deploying
the applications.
Connecting to ACME Observability and surfacing actionable data to the development
teams
You know the TVP works if you can use it to build and deploy changes to the IDP. It must lead
the way, ensuring that the other teams have as smooth an experience as possible.
After the TVP, the team had identified the next most important problem to solve, which would
make the second milestone. For an organization the size of ACME Financial Services, there
must be self-service capabilities. Without them upfront, the platform cannot scale, and the

Phase 2 would be characterized by many feedback loops, where the platform team made
changes, validated their success, and then either added new features or improved the existing
ones until it was possible for all application teams to leverage the platform. These regular
feedback loops were how the team could guarantee that the platform didn't just become a

The final capability the platform needed to have in this phase was cost management
capabilities. Uncontrolled costs were the catalyst for a platform, and so they could not be left
out. One of those capabilities was that it would manage the lifecycle of the observability data.
While there was an observability vendor in play, the IDP should act as a record of truth for how
the data in that vendor was managed through integration with the vendor. It needed to verify
and enforce that every application it knew about had a data sampling strategy in use and data
retention periods defined. For example, the policy might be that raw data is only retained for
180 days, and sampled data could be retained for 36 months, but only in cold storage, which is
less expensive. By ensuring that policies and capabilities existed and also following the
policies, the platform could become an effective cost management arm.
Unlike Phase 1, Phase 2 must have clear exit criteria:
Platform adoption had hit critical mass: ~60% of teams were using the IDP, and the rest
had a path forward to using it
Self-service capabilities existed, allowing teams to accelerate their own adoption and
add features
The platform was tracking costs, exposing the cost data, and had cost management-
related capabilities
ACME Observability was integrated with AI agents in use
The platform was acting as customer zero, ensuring that the golden paths remained
accessible for the rest of the company.

The final phase was the one that created the competitive edge. It was where the work that had
gone in up to then started to see the AI work as a force multiplier. That normalized data

The results of the presentation
The observability working group endured a difficult presentation with senior leadership. They
were challenged on the need for such drastic changes and the company reorganization that
would be required to support them. From senior leadership's initial position of reducing the
cost of the tooling, the proposal seemed far more expansive than was necessary.
However, as the presentation and resulting conversations progressed, senior leadership started
to see the need for the changes proposed. They especially liked the idea of metrics to be able to
track the impact of the changes, as well as addressing observability with a wider lens. As the
problems the working group uncovered became clearer to senior leadership, they slowly
started to come around to the changes they were being asked to support.
Senior leadership especially liked the parts of the plan that would expand the utility of ACME
Observability and the efforts to reduce cost. Their original ask was to investigate why the
expected cost savings hadn't materialized, but they also slowly started to realize that the scope
of the data they used to assess the effectiveness of the changes was too limited.
Unlike the first proposal from the observability working group, which was composed mostly of
minor changes and new tooling and required little of senior leadership, this proposal would
not reach its potential without significant support from senior leadership. Despite the initial
reluctance and resistance, senior leadership eventually came to accept and support the plan
presented by the observability working group. They accepted that there would not be a quick
resolution and the company was in for another multi-year journey, but they came to believe
that the end result would be a much stronger and more efficient company. They also believed
the new metrics would provide them with a much better understanding of where problems
and cost drivers existed within the company. Understanding what parts of the company are
involved in what business actions would also allow them to make better decisions.
To monitor the progress and impact of the changes, senior leadership required a dashboard to
be created with key performance indicators that they could follow. To start with, they wanted

Time jump: What was achieved
ACME Financial Services put the observability working group's proposal into motion, but due
to the changes in responsibilities and the creation of a new team or two, it took longer to
implement than the first proposal. Once the new teams were formed and leadership and
reporting structures put in place, it still took quite a while for the self-service systems to be
built and be ready for application teams to begin using them. These efforts represented the
foundation for the new process, and they did not happen quickly. This meant that senior
leadership had to be patient but also persistent to move the effort forward. It was a sometimes
delicate affair, but senior leadership's commitment to the plan proved critical to its success.
The patience was rewarded when application teams began to use the self-service tools. They
were able to deploy new versions faster with less effort, the telemetry data was standardized
and less expensive to process, and with the increased resources available to the application
teams, they were able to implement new features and fix bugs faster. The new metrics showed
an increase in the deployment velocity for every application team that used the self-service
tools.
The application developers were initially a bit confused about how to implement the principles
of observability-driven development, but after a few false starts, they really took them to heart
and began to see benefits via a reduction in the number of incidents and better suggestions and
help from the observability tooling. Having ACME Observability connected to the tools the
application developers already used allowed them to realize significant benefits without
having to drastically change their workflows. They even started using the observability tooling
to help proactively improve their designs and avert incidents before they occurred.
The time it took to create RCAs dropped dramatically. An SRE no longer had to dig through
mountains of logs and try to correlate application behavior to a deployment time. The SRE
could ask the observability platform to find the suspected root cause of the outage. Because the
observability platform was connected to the logs, metrics, deployment system, and source
code, it was able to return information about when an application was deployed, how it caused
the outage, and even point to the commit in the code repository that was deployed when the
outage occurred. All the SRE had to do was validate the information with what was already
known and ensure that the application developers agreed. It took some time, but both the SREs

Costs, which were the big driver for this effort, dropped. Not just the cost for running the tools,

Summary
In this chapter, we continued following ACME Financial Services' observability journey. They
discovered that their first attempt at fixing their problems by observing their systems was
really just the foundation for what needed to be achieved. The problems could not be solved
with just tools and some minor tweaks; they required significant support and focus within the
company in order to properly address them. They discovered they had been looking at
observability through too limited a lens, which caused them to miss seeing areas where the
new tools could help improve the company. They realized the current metrics used within the
company were insufficient to assess the benefits of the changes they were making, but with
new metrics and a broader view of observability, they were able to drive down operations costs
and support that effort with data. The end result was a more cost-effective and efficient
company with improved customer loyalty and reputation.

Architecture
In this chapter, we will learn how to build systems that leverage observability, AI, and
automation to reduce, or ideally eliminate, the number of business-impacting incidents.
Business-impacting incidents are situations that prevent an organization from operating cost-
efficiently, providing a highly resilient system that is available when users need it, and
ensuring that the system is secure and compliant with regulations.
We can leverage historical observability insights and use them to forecast future behavior to be
best prepared for situations that are likely to happen, for example, predictive scaling of critical
system components when end user load patterns change. We can use observability data of a
newly deployed release or enabled feature and have AI decide whether that code change is safe
to keep in production or whether it needs to be rolled back as it impacts performance,
scalability, or security. We can also use observability data to enable AI to make autonomous
decisions to redeploy workloads in different regions to save costs, optimize performance, or
block or redirect traffic that seems malicious.
This chapter will help you leap from using AI from the outside and instead move towards
putting AI at the center of your architecture. What would a system look like where AI makes
automated decisions on scaling or evolving a system? How would a self-driving IT architecture
benefit an organization?
In this chapter, we will cover the following topics:
Enabling AI-driven decision-making through event-driven architectures •
Use case: AI-driven scaling for performance and cost
Use case: AI and GitOps for rollouts and rollbacks

Technical requirements
This chapter discusses Argo CD, Jenkins, GitHub Actions, Kubernetes operations, and
HolmesGPT. There is no requirement to download or use any of these technologies in order to
understand the use cases and examples.

holmesgpt.dev/latest/

Defining our terms
Generally, the terms in this chapter should be fairly standard and well understood, so we won't
dive deeply into them, but we will add a quick review to ensure that there's a shared context for
readers as we progress through the chapter.
Differentiating proactive versus preventative versus self-
driven
In software operations, a proactive operation is one that is done in response to a signal, but
typically, the signal idx_e52196ae indicates there may be a problem, rather idx_2b509cf3 than that there is currently a

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera

problem, which would be reactive.
An example of a proactive action would be to take action against a system in response to a
metric. For example, memory consumption has reached 90% of the available RAM, so a
proactive action would be to increase the memory allocation so that there is not a memory-
related crash.
A preventative action would idx_90aa1903 be to find the cause idx_755a6cdc of the memory increase, especially if it was
sudden, and if necessary, write a fix that will allow memory usage to be lower or more
consistent, thereby preventing the need to scale.
A self-driven idx_e1ceb8bf architecture takes those same idx_645340c2 actions but fully automates them. In a self-driven
architecture, the metric is emitted, the scaling action happens, and then an automated RCA is
conducted, and a pull request is opened by an AI agent for a human to review and approve.

Could that ultimately be 100% AI end to end? Absolutely, but remember these technologies are
not without fault, and it's best for human supervision to be utilized for write actions. That
said, with human review at appropriate stages throughout the process, AI can make decisions
that help keep operations running smoothly, allowing more time for humans to innovate.
Enabling AI-driven decision-making through event-
driven architectures
Event-driven architectures are characterized by several services or microservices that either
emit idx_ba69fd68 or receive idx_599b26b3 events. The receiving service then performs a pre-defined action based on the
characteristics of the event it received. Essentially, this is metrics triggering automation: very
quick, very reliable, but also limited to what has been programmatically defined.
As we discussed in Chapter 2, the power of an LLM-based AI agent or assistant is that it's not
limited in the same way. However, it does still have limitations. Like humans, AI can only make
informed decisions when it has enough data points to tell it what the status is, what has
happened that led to this status, and what the options are to change this status when it is
undesired.
Feeding events into our observability platform
When we idx_d4e8c979 work to identify what events are worth collecting, the options can be overwhelming.
Fortunately, industry standards around key metrics have emerged as an excellent starting
point for developing your observability strategy.
If starting idx_1631c36c from zero, we recommend thinking about DORA metrics and Software
Development Life Cycle (SDLC) events.
Whether idx_c3aea70f it is Git, a CI/CD platform, testing tools, deployment and release tools, or
configuration change or feature flag management tools. They all typically provide a way to
send webhooks to external tools for integration purposes.
Let's take Argo CD as an example. Argo CD provides a notification feature where details about
every sync stage – PreSync, SyncStart, SyncFinished, and SyncFailed – can be sent via a
webhook. Sending this to your observability platform is therefore a simple configuration task,
but one that provides detailed information about which Git commit was successfully synced by
Argo CD to the target environment. This functionality is not unique to Argo CD and, therefore,
the Kubernetes ecosystem; the same capabilities can be leveraged via most CI/CD platforms or
configuration change management systems.
Jenkins, for example, supports plugins, much like Argo CD. One of those plugins is an
OpenTelemetry connector, which can connect to multiple observability backends. While you

may see Jenkins in Kubernetes (there's a flavor of it called Kubernetes Jenkins), Jenkins is often

GitHub Actions, which idx_4eaf6428 are architecture agnostic, can similarly leverage webhooks via the open
source project Workflow Webhook (https://github.com/distributhor/workflow-
webhook).
Feature idx_dad006e7 flag management tools follow the same general capability patterns, with feature
flagging SDKs such as OpenFeature also emitting OpenTelemetry spans, logs, and metrics in
the application that implements the feature behind a flag. This allows an operator (human or
AI) to identify which feature flags were enabled on a request-by-request basis, as this
information shows up on the distributed trace spans as span attributes. This level of detail
allows us to come to a conclusion on who is impacted by a bad feature, as explained in the
previous section.
Thanks to open standard initiatives, we see more tool vendors not only supporting generic
webhook interfaces but also webhooks that provide data adhering to semantic conventions as
defined by OpenTelemetry, CDEvents, or SDLC events.
Scenario: tying events and AI operations together
In Chapter 3, in the Context is king: the quality of observability data section, we learned about how
important it is to have context-enriched observability data. The more information about idx_63491ce9 your
data centers, hosts, clusters, processes, workloads, and services we have, the easier it is to
derive the status quo.
In the sub-section called Enriching observability data across the software development lifecycle, we
talked about how to have all tools that take part in the software development process (version
control, building, testing, CI/CD, infrastructure automation, release management, and so on)
send events to the observability platform through standardized SDLC events. This provides
additional context for a human operator, but also for an AI agent to learn about things such as
the following:

How AI can help us analyze the situation
When an anomaly happens, such as an increase in failure rate or response time, a human
operator idx_fccd851d would look at all the available data to determine whether this anomaly is caused by
any known event. In complex systems, this may take a significant amount of time to connect all
the dots and draw all the right conclusions. In a distributed system, the data may also be
distributed across multiple locations as well as data types (logs, metrics, and traces).
When feeding all this data to AI, it can collect and analyze that same data in seconds and tell us
the following:
Intermittent response time issues are only happening for requests that execute the code
paths of the feature flag that was enabled recently
Based on the pull request and feature flag change details, this only impacts a single
customer
This customer typically starts becoming active shortly after 6 a.m. on a workday
When forecasting that all expected login requests from that customer will get slower,
the noisy neighbor effect means it will impact the overall performance and stability of
the authentication service
Seeing all this evidence, the logical next steps would be the following:
Turn off the feature flag to reduce the risk of potential bigger impact.
Open a new pull request for the engineering team referencing PR-242 and providing
logs, metrics, and traces that show the production impact.
Run a code analysis and provide a potential fix based on the runtime behavior.
Notify the development team that merged PR-242 about the situation.
Taking those actions puts the teams in a much better position than waiting until the problem
spreads! But how exactly do we get AI engaged?
How to let the AI also take automated actions
Sending all this data to the observability platform is the basis for better root cause analysis. But
it also idx_dabc7d9b provides the basis for taking automated actions.
When a feature flag is turned on and causes issues, we can leverage the feature flagging
management tool's API to turn off that feature flag automatically. If the deployment of a new
release has a negative impact, we can roll back to the previous version.
For possible scenarios where an incident could occur, we can define remediation actions that
should be executed. These could be in the form of another automation pipeline or a script that
mitigates any issues caused by a change that had negative impacts.

Use case: AI and GitOps
GitOps isn't just idx_dc69c9d9 continuous deployment. It's the process of continuous reconciliation of
desired and actual state. Once we understand that, the additional possibilities are nearly
endless.
Imagine you idx_30bdf91f are deploying a mission-critical application in a Kubernetes environment. If you
have a Service-Level Objective (SLO) of 99.99%, you need to have automated failure
detection and self-healing.
This is another idx_26bff8a7 place where AI and GitOps can be very powerful. So, imagine having your AI
agent running alongside your GitOps systems with all the proper RBAC to investigate and
resolve complications as they arise.
Integrating agentic AI for Kubernetes
To demonstrate an agentic AI implementation, we'll discuss HolmesGPT. HolmesGPT is an
open source AI SRE agent (https://github.com/HolmesGPT/holmesgptP) that is also a Cloud
Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) sandbox project. For local use, the HolmesGPT CLI
can idx_c2ed78bb be installed via Homebrew and configured to work with one or multiple providers, such as
OpenAI or Ollama. For an integration idx_c0350258 and fully agentic system, you can install it via a Helm
chart. Either way, when you install HolmesGPT, you also get the ability to invoke HolmesGPT
via an HTTP API.
As magical as AI feels, it's not entirely magic, so here we'll see how AI integrates with simple
automation to do more.

Chapter 8 284
Integration with GitOps and troubleshooting a rollout failure is just one of many possible use
cases for full agentic operations. When identifying where to start in your own services, you
may decide to instead use the approach of troubleshooting specific alerts. Regardless of where
you start, we recommend implementing the read and investigate actions first, and after you
idx_bcfe3cbe have confidence in your configurations and runbooks, expanding to the automated
remediations as well.
Our next use case is closely related to GitOps and uses somewhat similar workflows, so let's
have a look.
Use case: AI-driven scaling for performance and cost
After reaching out to experts across the industry, one idx_a47e6ae3 common thread we found was that AI is
being leveraged significantly for scaling use cases.
Types of scaling
There are two types of scaling in computing: vertical and horizontal. Vertical scaling is the
process idx_537a7a3e of scaling up in place. In other words, expanding or reducing the size of a disk, adding
CPU or memory to a virtual machine, and so on. Horizontal scaling is the process of adding or
removing an additional copy of the resource you're measuring. That could be another set of
Pods, another Kubernetes node, another virtual machine, or another load balancer, as
examples. However you choose to scale, your scaling strategy needs to be intentional and tied
to the business needs.
Scaling for performance
Scaling for idx_b60f03d9 performance means keeping the system resources balanced so that applications are
as performant as possible. Imagine a basic queue. You can set a threshold that, if exceeded,
then another thread pool is created to work through the queue items. In most cases, for scaling,
simple automation does the trick; however, that automation is typically reactive. With AI
available to parse large amounts of data and identify possible patterns, you can go from
reactive to proactive. For example, financial institutions may notice a sharp uptick in traffic as
the stock markets open on Monday mornings. Agentic systems can proactively scale
environments up a little ahead of this spike, so that price information, trade information, or
any other type of system interaction is always as fast as possible. If traffic patterns change, the
agentic system will detect these new patterns and adjust accordingly, as opposed to a human
operator regularly tracking these patterns and updating automated thresholds.
285 Evolving Operations: Proactive > Preventive > Self-Driven Architecture
Scaling for cost
Scaling for cost can mean scaling back down to save on cloud bills. For example, if we expand
on idx_30b7d659 our previous example of scaling up when the stock market trading is going to start, we can
also do the reverse. Scaling back down during traffic lulls can keep costs down, and AI can do

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 284
chunks.content:
this faster and more regularly than a human can. However, we can also rebalance our
workloads to run on hardware that is cheaper. By augmenting our AI capabilities with an
understanding of cloud options, cloud spend, and desired outcomes, we can have it regularly
review and make suggestions about the environment for how to reduce costs or proactively
take actions such as spinning up cheaper Kubernetes Node types and migrating workloads as
desired.
This can be as simple as using Kubernetes Jobs, or another scheduling system (Jenkins, Tekton,
Argo Workflows, Apache Airflow, cron jobs, or something else) to regularly invoke the AI
system to do a review and either take action or make a recommendation.
However you choose to accomplish this, the type of data review and decisions required to
maintain system scale are the exact types of tasks AI excels at.
Scaling for carbon footprint
Related to scaling for cost, but also somewhat separate, is the idea of scaling to help reduce the
carbon idx_78ea7e07 footprint of applications. With many localities working towards improving their
carbon footprint (see The Paris Agreement), open source projects have started to come forward
to help specifically observe the carbon footprint of systems. The idx_75b0ab9c first example of this is Kepler
(https://www.cncf.io/projects/kepler/), which provides eBPF-based energy insights.
According to the official documentation:
Kepler (Kubernetes-based Efficient Power Level Exporter) is a Prometheus exporter that measures
energy consumption at the container, Pod, VM, and process level by reading hardware sensors and
attributing power based on resource utilization.
Kepler uses Intel RAPL (Running Average Power Limit) sensors to collect energy data from CPU
packages, cores, and memory subsystems, then distributes this energy proportionally to workloads
based on their CPU time consumption.
But getting data is only part of managing your CO2 emissions. There needs to be a
corresponding idx_93f23d99 action. Here, the kube-green operator helps you reduce CO2 emissions by
putting Pods to sleep that are not needed: https://kube-green.dev/.
Both of these projects are a step in the right direction. While agentic AI isn't necessarily
immediately considered environmentally friendly, responsible AI use can be part of how your
organization manages its carbon footprint.

Chapter 8 286
Since AI can parse large amounts of data quickly, it can also help with data management. Large
amounts of data sitting in storage can be expensive to store and computationally expensive to
parse. But if you can audit your data store with AI, it can help you to clean up unnecessary data
and assist with data sampling to ensure you're storing and reading only what you need, and
not what you don't.
This also idx_f638dffe helps reduce your surface area for risk related to data breaches if you've normalized
and reduced your overall data overhead. Again, you can write and deploy automation to do all
of this as well; however, this requires custom programming of all the possible actions and
regularly re-deploying as you add more, whereas agentic AI can follow instructions, safety
guardrails, and dynamically adjust to system needs, closing the loop on time to successfully
benefit from possible efficiency gains.
How to approach auto scaling
In order to get started with scaling, we need to know, or be able to calculate, two things: where
we idx_42d86943 are starting and where we are going. That means, first and foremost, we need to have
benchmarks for our system. When we know what the minimum load looks like and what the
maximum load looks like, we know the range through which we need to scale. This helps us
predict our costs as well. Next, or additionally, since this can be done at the same time, we need
to have a history of load. Very few systems experience consistent traffic 24/7; they're usually
more active during certain hours than others. That history and the threshold information can
be used to train an AI agent so that it can help determine patterns and optimal times for
scaling.
With the model trained, it needs to have some way of interfacing with the scaling
orchestration mechanism. This is where an MCP server would be used to help the AI agent
interface with the scaling system and utilize it. Lastly, apply guardrails. Don't allow the agent
to scale a system endlessly, since there could be a problem that needs attention if scaling up
and up is continuously required.
Some vendors of cloud solutions are already offering this capability as part of their existing
solutions, so it's important to have a build versus buy conversation and determine whether
this is a capability you need to build bespoke or leverage from an existing vendor or tool within
your ecosystem.
Now it's time to look at the final use case for this chapter: agentic AI as a security helper.
287 Evolving Operations: Proactive > Preventive > Self-Driven Architecture
Enemy at the gates: let your AI be your defender
In Chapter 5, we talked about data cardinality being a key aspect of AI inference success. This is
critical again for using AI to assist with detecting possible security incidents. A big clue to an AI

chunks.content:
agent that something is amiss is if there's suddenly data that doesn't match the patterns and
standards of the data typically seen across the system.
Using AI to parse audit logs and system access
For example, in Kubernetes audit logs, the IP address of the user agent and source IP address
idx_efc14010 that reached out to the API server are recorded, in addition to the user or entity that made the
request.
Imagine a credential is leaked via phishing, but our security team doesn't know that yet.
However, our AI watcher has identified that the source IP of an API call is significantly different
this time than previous times for the same user. It can flag this activity and open a security
incident through the appropriate ticketing system or workflow. If it's an agentic
implementation, it may also have the capabilities to reduce or remove the permissions of that
user account until after the activity has been confirmed.
In another case, let's imagine a trade embargo. This is where trade is restricted between
countries; financial transactions, as well as software and digital media, are included in these
restrictions. Enforcing these embargos is critical for any system with an international presence.
Agentic AI can watch various configurations simultaneously, including firewalls, to ensure the
configurations are enforcing the latest trade rules.
But this won't necessarily work if the person trying to get around the embargo is using a VPN.
Agentic AI can help again here, by checking the source IPs against known VPN provider IP
pools, and flagging or blocking the traffic.
But what happens if you do have a breach? What is your risk vector? How much liability might
you have?
AI for reducing risk surface area
In order idx_1f26fa91 to reduce your surface area for risk, you first must identify what that risk surface area
is. The best way to do this is to conduct a threat model. For the best guidance on how to
conduct a good threat model, we recommend OWASP as the authoritative resource (https://
owasp.org/www-community/Threat_Modeling).

Risk surface 1: data
In most software systems, the data collected and stored is the most valuable asset. But that
data can idx_9db30c9f also contain data that is regulated. PII or Personally Identifiable Data is regulated
heavily in many countries and localities, and so idx_8f8bb699 must be handled with great care. While it's
possible for a vendor system where you might store or use your data to come with all the
security and compliance requirements for you to ship your data raw, it's a much better practice
to sanitize your data of PII. For this, we would not recommend a cloud-based AI vendor. Run a
local model that is self-contained to help you identify and strip any potential PII from logs.
For this example, we used HolmesGPT on our laptop. We provided system logs along with the
prompt Analyze these logs and remove PII and surface only logs that look like they could be related to
system crashes or performance issues. The model returned two log results that contained possible
matches for the criteria, and all PII was removed.
Figure 8.2: HolmesGPT sanitized log results
These results are only a very small percentage of the log lines provided, and if stored, would
take up very little space and be easily indexed and accessed, while also not creating exposure
for any unnecessary risks around PII in the data contents.
While it is a best practice that application logs are sanitized and only as noisy as needed, and
there are also times to keep PII around, using AI as a failsafe to ensure an organization only has
what it needs to have on hand is a smart use of a powerful tool that could potentially save you
from a lot of liability.
289 Evolving Operations: Proactive > Preventive > Self-Driven Architecture
Risk surface 2: users and permissions
In an IDP where there are many users onboarding with various needs and access levels, it's
important idx_fce2a05c to do a regular review of who has access and what they have access to. However,
depending on the size of the organization, this could be a very difficult task. Fortunately,
parsing through lots of information quickly is exactly what your AI tools are purpose-built to
accomplish. Having an AI assistant or agent review users and their access, under the
supervision of a human operator, can quickly help to identify whether there are users, human
or otherwise, with access levels that don't match best practices, may be too permissive, or who
need to be offboarded entirely.
With these things in mind, and understanding how we can integrate agentic AI into our
systems, let's look at a more complete use case for AI-assisted security.

workloads

Chain of custody explained
The chain idx_a5dc9652 of custody is the record of the idx_7b7afd4c hands through which a product passes before it
reaches its final destination. In software, this is also called the software supply chain. This
includes every line of code from every source that contributes to the final product, such as the
language the code is written in and imported libraries. This representation is typically done idx_4347320e as
a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), covered in Chapter 9. An SBOM shows you what imports
you have, but doesn't validate the veracity of the images. This is what Cosign or other tools
accomplish.
Commit signing and signature verification
When writing secure software, it's important to verify the identities of the people who are
pushing idx_a88fd691 the code. This is why many organizations have added pre-commit webhooks to
repositories to require that all commits are signed idx_7983e4c0 with the unique signature of the committer.
This uses GNU Privacy Guard (GPG) cryptographic keys, where the private key is how idx_a53bc80f the
commit is signed, and the public key allows others to verify that signature.
The public key needs to be in the keyring of the local filesystem where the signature is being
verified. GitHub helps do all of this for you, but it can be set up for private Git instances as well.
Reputable idx_9c38170f providers of open source packages will sign those packages. The Cosign project from
Sigstore (https://www.sigstore.dev/) is a free and open source software package designed
precisely to combat supply chain attacks and risks. The three main attack vectors image

Typosquatting: Malicious idx_22b669a9 packages with deliberately similar names to common
packages
Compromised hosts: Where idx_3d0eef42 the package is made publicly available, the host machine
itself could be compromised and serve up incorrect images in an attempt to get
malicious packages onto new machines
Artifact tampering: Where idx_1041a952 the valid artifact is altered and then re-published to trick
users into compromised software
Reputable vendors of images will sign these images. Those signatures will include attestations
on the build process, contents, and security. A best security practice is to include a signing step
in your CI/CD pipelines for any images and artifacts built within your organization, as well as
to validate that the images being used in your environment are legitimate. You can use Cosign
both to sign and validate signatures.

Validating package contents
If you idx_af1dfe2d need to validate a package's integrity, you idx_24c63da4 can look at the hash of the package, generated
with Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA) libraries and typically with the SHA-256 algorithm. The
generated hash, which is immutable, becomes a reference to a point in time of the software. If
the software in the package changes, the hash changes. For example, if I download the latest
Python today and compare it to the latest from last year, they have different hashes. They are
often just referred to as SHAs, as a reference to the hashing algorithm.
To validate idx_86383067 software packages, run a checksum comparison. Checksum is a tool that allows you
to get the SHA-256 output for a local package. By running checksum or shasum against the local
copy of the package and comparing it to the published version, you can validate that the
package is as expected. This is easier for some files than others, and if you have modified the
package in any way, it will fail. An example of an expected failure would be that Python
publishes an expected SHA-256 for each version release, but the Linux distribution Fedora will
re-package the upstream version, causing your shasum or checksum to fail, so take care to
validate against the proper source of truth.
In the case of containerized environments such as Podman, Docker, or Kubernetes, you can
often reference specific image digests via the SHA to ensure you always get the exact same
software every time.

Use case: repository maintenance – let AI take on
the boring tasks
In every software engineering project, there are chores that need to be done regularly. One of
the most common is idx_aaeeed20 dependency management; tools such as Dependabot are often leveraged
for simple automation to bump up versions of dependencies imported into a project. However,
in situations where the dependency-related code has idx_746aeb48 been copied directly into the repository,
that won't work. Instead, the local copy of the code needs to be replaced. This concept exists in
many languages, but we'll focus on the Golang implementation of vendoring for this example.
Vendoring is different idx_6c6dad4b from a typical import of an external dependency as, instead of the
dependencies being brought in during compilation or at runtime, the vendored code lives as a
copy in the project repository. Vendoring can be seen in many open source projects, specifically
in the Kubernetes space. However, despite the benefits of having a local version of the
dependency pinned exactly where you might want it, it's not ideal from a security standpoint.
You still need to update packages for CVEs and to get the latest features and functionality.
When to do this depends entirely on when the vendored project releases a new version, but the
how is very straightforward. However, it is tedious. This is where we can let our AI agents and
assistants do the work for us.
If you had an internal project vendored and a new release of that project became available, you
would want to test that release as soon as possible. However, this typically requires checking
out the code, manually updating the go.mod file to the newest release, running the go mod
vendor command, and then doing any other chores before running tests. If the tests pass, then
you would want to open a pull request and likely begin a new release of your code base as well.
This can be solved with automation, but it can be unwieldy to build and maintain.
Alternatively, you can use instruction files, as we discussed in Chapter 5, and GitHub Actions to
accomplish it with an AI agent.

perform the actions only if there's a new release. The basic architecture of this GitHub

designed with observability-driven development. Each metric helps to build trust at varying

Response accuracy

For AIOps systems, these metrics can be directly mapped back to specific business values and
risks. In the following section, we'll take a look at each of these one by one, including what
their business value is, and what risk tracking this metric can mitigate.
While the consequences of inaccuracy in AI systems are always going to be present, there's an
increased surface area for risk in AIOps as opposed to, say, an AI meeting transcript or an AI
chatbot, as neither of these could inadvertently delete a production database.
We covered natural language process scoring in Chapter 5, but we didn't cover all the ways to
use that scoring or gain confidence. There are additional methods to mix and match
programmatic scoring and idx_ff7288e8 human sentiment to create your final bar for measuring accuracy, as
well. Let's look at those other methods now.
Regular dry runs
Dry runs go hand in hand with any alert tuning or accuracy grading that you may decide on.
Instead of waiting for real incidents to idx_dbcf392d occur to investigate, you can instead have the system
tell you what it would do if one were occurring. You'd then compare the response against the
provided runbooks or against human knowledge. You can spin up sandbox environments to
create scenarios against which you can automate the validation of these dry runs by giving
your AI agent regular prompts and validating that the responses match expectations.

Leveraging vendors and tools
AI vendors dedicate immense time and resources to providing accurate models, and they have
the expertise to do so. Since ensuring accuracy is a mission-critical part of running an AIOps
implementation, it's reasonable to offload that burden to a trusted vendor, especially if you're
already in their ecosystem. Vendors have optimized their leveraged AI models for the use case
around understanding observability idx_5c1aa6bb data, detecting and explaining problems, and
recommending the right actions to remediate. Here is a brief list of vendors and their
capabilities:
Dynatrace provides Dynatrace Intelligence with a variety of AI capabilities to detect
root cause, explain impact, and idx_99c2d028 execute agentic actions for remediation. The platform
allows you to define your own agentic workflows. It takes your idx_bf735fc4 observability data into
account when answering questions, and you can define your own instructions as part

automated root cause analysis.
New Relic provides New Relic AI, which acts as an observability assistant for
analyzing, troubleshooting, and idx_78a9d746 querying system data using natural language.
Meanwhile, the open source software community has created several notable projects as well:
Robusta, which has both an idx_b9dcfda3 open source offering and a paid offering, integrates with
HolmesGPT, which they also idx_dd4a8820 created and made open source. Robusta is an
observability platform with an AI agent, not an AI platform, making it more purpose-
built.
LangChain provides a fully open source framework for LLM applications, and their free
and paid offerings idx_15cb3cf4 include evaluation tools idx_384fe2a3 such as LangSmith to help you observe
your model accuracy.
Agenta, as previously idx_28c05313 mentioned, has many capabilities.
DeepEval was demonstrated idx_f47e84d1 earlier in this chapter.
Ragas is an evaluation idx_fca0f83d pipeline for RAG and LLM AI systems.
However you decide to approach observing and managing model accuracy, there are many
options to help you go from just getting started, to being ready for production.
When building your own solution, it is advisable to get some inspiration from the observability
vendors as they have purposely optimized their built-in AI and agentic workflows for the key
observability use cases around: understanding observability data, explaining root causes,
coming up with potential remediation actions, and integrating with an ecosystem that can also
execute remediation actions. In either case, it's important that you start experimenting with
those systems, learn how effective they are, and start tweaking them to your needs.
Accuracy is an important metric for building trust because an accurate system is less likely to
make mistakes. But no system will be error-free, which is why it's also important to design and
implement governance to act as guardrails for your AI agent.
Implementing and observing governance
Ideally, your AI agent shouldn't be able to delete a database any more than your AI meeting
assistant can. To ensure that, guardrails must be put into place around the implementation of
any agentic AI to ensure that certain actions are not attempted or allowed. If there is an
attempt, whether these attempted idx_5ffbda3b actions are user-initiated is also important.

While access controls to the AI systems are also mission-critical, we will cover those more in

the Securing the AI section later in this chapter.
A guardrail is a policy idx_10f25856 enforcement mechanism that blocks an action that would be considered
unsafe. In Kubernetes, there are many ways of controlling what can happen. Role-based
access control (RBAC), policy engines, and validating webhooks can all prevent actions from
being taken entirely or by idx_1474da0f underprivileged users and service accounts. If you have this access
and policies configured, your Kubernetes observability stack will easily be able to track when
someone or something is trying to exceed its permissions levels. You can also make the AI
agent aware of the policies it needs to adhere to by including the policies in all instruction files,
but it would be dangerous to allow it to be self policing without any other enforcement arm.
Fortunately, you can place guardrails and audit whether they've been necessary at every level
of your technical stack.
Guardrails in the cloud
Starting from the top and going down the stack idx_28a20fcb from there, for your cloud-based deployments,
the major cloud providers (Azure, Google Cloud, and AWS) all have methods of identity and
access management (IAM) for workloads as well idx_60aa020b as for humans. This allows you to assign
your AI agent an identity and scope of permissions that it would not be able to exceed. Any
attempts to exceed policy would be identifiable in the cloud's logging. For example, AWS
CloudTrail stores these interactions as events.
For AWS, IAM and Security Token Service (STS) are the idx_e8b20823 governing technologies. For Azure,
workload identities (including managed identities, service principals, and applications) are
critical for identity governance, while Azure Policy helps enforce governance across the cloud
environment. In Google Cloud, workload identities are the long-established practice, alongside
service accounts, but they also have agent identities specific to agentic AI workloads. These
identities are tied specifically to the AI agent they are created for, and are lifecycled alongside
it, meaning that if it goes away, so does the identity. This means if you change out your agent,
you'll have a new identity to go along with it. For the most up-to-date information on each idx_91cdfcd5 of
these technologies, refer to the official documentation for your cloud provider.

Chapter 9 306
These cloud governance technologies can be used for traditional cloud deployments,
serverless, and also Kubernetes-based environments. Ensuring the correct capabilities and
permissions at every level is an architecture-agnostic best practice.
Regardless of which cloud and what methods you're using to enforce least privilege for your AI
agent, you will have the ability to audit and flag any attempts at exceeding the defined scope of
the AI agent.
Guardrails as middleware
Kubernetes RBAC services, admission controllers, validating webhooks, and policy engines are
an excellent example of middleware that would be used to prevent AI misuse or misbehavior.
These intercept network traffic to the idx_bd45294f final destination and can accept or reject it based on the
parameters of the policies they're programmed against.
For example, if you've given the AI agent read-only permissions against a cluster and it tries to
delete a Pod, the RBAC service on your cluster will prevent it, and you can use webhooks or log
forwarding to capture that the denied action was attempted.
When you're not in a Kubernetes environment (or even when you are), the same patterns apply
at the application level. In your system design, middleware will sit between the AI and all
network traffic, evaluating prompts before they reach the agent, and responses before they're
returned. A simple API gateway implementation can be used for this, but AI gateways are
becoming a more readily available tool.
We'll use Kong, an open source idx_de255c5f and SaaS offering that provides API gateways and AI gateways
for serverless and Kubernetes deployments. While you can use the open source version to self-
host, we chose to use their hosted version for demonstration purposes.

Another open source AI idx_b7187c66 gateway option is LiteLLM (https://docs.litellm.ai/docs). In

Whether you build your own API gateway from scratch or implement a solution from the

Demonstrating success
If you want to build a system that will be trusted, build a system against which you can
measure success. In Chapter 2, we discussed the importance of OKRs and KPIs. These are very
important, but they are part of a big picture. For getting started and building a technical
roadmap, it's important to start smaller.
Identify one or two problems that are in search of a solution where AI can reasonably be that

solution. Then, design your MVP implementation. Don't try to solve problems you might have;
just solve the ones you've identified. Once you have your MVP in place, iterate. Talk to
stakeholders or subject matter experts, identify what other problems could be solved by
integration with an AIOps solution, and build your technical roadmap based on those user
interviews.
User stories are a great way to build a technical roadmap, but use whatever method works best
for your team, as long as the method is evidence-based.

Reliability
A trustworthy system is a reliable system. While we have already discussed this to some
degree, most measurements of AIOps systems we've covered measure performance.
Performance and reliability are related, but are not the same thing. For example, a successful
communication with my OpenAI assistant through the Kong gateway had a latency of 1,516 ms,
which is about 1.5 seconds. This was very quick from an end user perspective and should be
considered a good idx_10659f1a response time for an AI interaction. However, in order to demonstrate
reliability, I would need to benchmark many more requests that returned within a timeframe
that provided a good user experience. In general, times between 1 and 3 seconds would be
considered performant, 5 to 10 might be concerning depending on the task, and over 10 is
probably worthy of concern. These performance metrics can give us an idea of our system's
reliability.
These response times would be an idx_f2b92322 example of a service-level indicator (SLI). These SLIs are
data points that help us put together an overall picture. A service-level objective (SLO) is a idx_0367a180
measurement of reliability. It's an aggregation of SLIs over time, or performance over time.
While sudden spikes or drops in some metrics may indicate a reliability issue and are worthy of
kicking off an alert or incident, a steady increase in response latency over time is also worthy of
an alert. Another way of looking at it is, if we know what our performance should be, and we
can measure when we're not hitting those targets, then we know whether our system is
reliable or not. A reliable system is a delightful system that gains and retains users.
A system that delights users probably idx_c50c1b10 has a good return on investment (ROI). However, that
may not always be the case, which is why we must still be aware of costs and cost management
strategies.
The hidden costs of implementing AI
It's important when idx_a3ca2238 going into an AI implementation to not be caught unaware of the
potential costs of the implementation. AI has specific hardware requirements, and the price
model for paying for it via vendors has a unique economy.
Tokens and AI costs
There's an economic principle that says There ain't no such thing as a free lunch. While it's true
that AI can feel like magic and can quickly generate helpful outputs, you are paying for that
functionality. The goal of a idx_0ae93d28 successful AI implementation should be that when a cost-benefit
analysis is done, the solution provides more value than it costs to run.
Just like it's important to keep track of spending with any infrastructure project, it's also
important to track and understand token usage.
313 No Future Without Challenges
Tokens and spending
When working with vendors in this space, there's a cost per token that typically is what creates

brings us back to the importance of observing our AI. When we have the token counts, we can
also report on costs. There are many tools out there that provide this type of data. If you're
using a vendor, they may help you to track and visualize this data. For example, Kong and

Token management
Tokens used are not just money spent. When using a vendor-supplied model, tokens and
money are definitely one and idx_2124a567 the same, but for a local model, that's not the case. Tokens build
up the context of the conversation. When you start a new session with an AI agent or assistant,
there is no context and therefore no token in use. For example, if the very first question asked of
DeepSeek in a new session is about token usage, it won't have any data. Instead, it will tell you
about tokens in general and how it can help you understand your token usage:
Figure 9.6: DeepSeek explaining tokens
This is true for multiple sessions and for multiple users, hence the importance of using
observability tools to capture and track token usage in order to manage costs. When you're
communicating with an AI model via an API, each response may have a token count that you
would want to collect and aggregate, but it's unlikely to have an aggregated count ready for
any users who might be using the model. Thus, having all usage routed through a centralized
platform or API gateway will allow you to gain those observability insights in order to track
usage and spend.
We discussed this in Chapter 2, but as a reminder, outside of acting as a billing metric, tokens
serve another, even more important, purpose as well. Tokens are the unit of measurement for
the total amount of data the model can handle before you will see performance issues. This
limit is known as the context window. After idx_2693be36 that threshold is exceeded, the model is likely to
start forgetting or become more error-prone.
That's why, for cost control and system health, token management must be a key part of your
AI implementation strategy.
Thanks to OpenLLMetry, we get enriched OpenTelemetry data, including prompts, tokens,
temperature, and all sorts of other metadata when calling an LLM:
317 No Future Without Challenges
Figure 9.7: OpenLLMetry data capture
You can use this data in conjunction with an API or AI gateway to capture usage, track spend,
set and enforce rate limits, as idx_b07431d7 well as quota or caps. LiteLLM and Kong both also have these
capabilities for capturing telemetry and enforcing quota, making either of them a good option
for adoption within an organization. They are not the only gateway solutions out there; you
may find one from another vendor that better fits your needs or budget, or you may determine
that building something yourself is better.
Regardless of building or buying a solution, it's important that you get the right thing. We'll
look more at other aspects of tokens and managing them for AI systems, which we hope will
help you to be successful in whatever approach you take.
Prompt engineering and context engineering
In Chapter 2, when looking at prompt engineering, we shared some examples of prompts made

chunks.heading: Chapter 9 316
chunks.content:
better by asking AI how to make them better. Included in this was asking AI to help optimize
our prompt for token usage. Getting a idx_8d29334a high-value, low-token prompt can be an easy way to
help manage token use. For an AIOps system where you may have an SRE agent or other
implementations, you'll likely see the same prompt used and reused, which is different from an
assistant or chatbot, where prompts are less static. Taking the time to optimize your prompts
for token consumption while still getting the accurate responses you need will be time well
spent.
However, we can also include in idx_9e5f3b9e our prompt that we want the AI agent to be token-conscious
in its responses as well. This can supplement model settings and environment configurations,
such as token caps. Additionally, prompt compression is another technique that can be used

to help reduce the number of tokens in prompts. This is especially useful for user-generated
prompts where you cannot control the input, only seek to make it more cost-efficient.
Prompt compression tools such as LLMLingua (https://github.com/microsoft/LLMLingua),
which is idx_b943defe available under the MIT license, use an SLM to analyze a prompt and reduce the token
count by summarizing the prompt without dropping critical information or context. For short
prompts, this isn't going to make too much difference, but for logs and observability data
where the data inputs, especially for streaming telemetry, can quickly become massive, this is a
powerful addition to your AIOps stack to ensure that you get the most value with the least
spend, and without overloading your LLM, causing it to hallucinate or error. An AI gateway can
help you with integrating prompt compression, and it is a feature of Kong as a configurable
plugin.
Figure 9.8: Kong prompt compressor plugin UI
Prompt compression is part of a larger group of practices, all categorized as context
engineering. Context engineering essentially is idx_30919378 a set of practices that help you keep your AI
systems running well by protecting the context window from being exceeded. Two other
practices are compaction and pruning.
Pruning is the removal of old idx_7aa6e0fb context that we no longer care about or unimportant
information. For example, if I delete a Kubernetes Pod, I can tell my LLM to delete all
information it knows about that. That data is irrelevant but could become a ghost in the
machine, leaving my AIOps idx_748d7f80 systems to believe the lack of new data about it is an error, or to
possibly even hallucinate based on what it knew about the workload that's now gone. But even
when something is still relevant, we can and should prune the context of the least valuable
data. For example, if we are troubleshooting an issue in a Kubernetes cluster, we may have an
alert against a namespace, but it's likely not the only namespace we'll need to look in. Our AI
agent may need to see what namespaces exist, but once it identifies the important ones, it
doesn't need to maintain that information. Dropping the irrelevant pieces of context from the
session will help keep the context window smaller. You can also have it take structured notes
so that if anything happens to the session, such as a network interruption, you can give it the
319 No Future Without Challenges
notes file and pick back up where you left off. This allows for minimal context and helps you to
use fewer tokens.
Pruning is also highly useful for RAG systems. The documents that may be called could be quite
large or repetitive. Pruning tools will preprocess those documents before feeding them to the
LLM, allowing for fewer tokens to be necessary for the same amount of work. Many of the

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 318
chunks.content:
machine learning technologies have some capability for pruning. If you're using a RAG system,
you can implement pruning into the neural network. For Claude users, they've added the
capability to prune context from the model.
Compaction is somewhat similar to idx_ca599e7e pruning in that it will reduce the information in the
context window, but the mechanism and timing will be different. Compaction takes a
conversation or context that is approaching the context limit and summarizes it. Next, a new
context window is established with that summary supplied as the basis for what is effectively a
new session. Pruning and compaction can and should be used in harmony to help reduce the
risk of errors or hallucination. Some users may find that incorrect pruning can lead to garbled
context and, therefore, errors, whereas compaction will help maintain a more accurate context
despite needing to establish a new one. Both pruning and compaction can be used together,
and you may find options for both built into vendors for AI models.
An example of this can be found within the Robusta platform (https://robusta.dev).
Robusta has built compaction into its offering for HolmesGPT, along with tracking of the
current context window's capacity and a breakdown of how the context was used.

Where a vendor isn't in use, or you have teams that are not data science experts, an SLM as a
middle layer to assist with pruning or compaction will probably be just as effective as other
options. The fact that managing tokens well also helps to lower costs is an important point in
favor of doing so, but likely less important than the gains to model accuracy or reliability.
Keeping token use low is a key optimization aspect of AI utilization, which can be fully realized
alongside other benefits via fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning
Fine-tuning is a hidden cost because it may require computational resources and human time
you might not have idx_726c0a42 accounted for when setting off to integrate AI into your work stream.
Before your AIOps system is truly ready for production, you will need to ensure that it's been
properly idx_24c265da fine-tuned. GPTs are models that are pretrained, so although they may be better
suited to the business case they've been trained for than a model without a GPT, they do not
necessarily absolve you of the need to further tune your language model. And while you may
find even more success out of the gate with a purpose-built model supplied by a idx_9a5988ef vendor, you
may still need to refine it for your specific environment.
Fine-tuning does not mean replacing the training data or adjusting all the data and parameters
within the model. It's supplementary guidance to help govern how your LLM approaches your
problems. If we think of it like a building, it's an adjustment to the facade, while leaving the
original structure intact.
There is not just one way to fine-tune, and some of the ways can be dependent on how you
decide to deploy your AI solution. However, generally speaking, Jupyter Notebook (https://
docs.jupyter.org/en/latest/) is considered an industry standard for model fine-tuning and
working with Ollama and the other AI technologies we've been demonstrating throughout the
book.
While fine-tuning is often necessary, it can take a significant period of time to get right. It's
also not a task that ever ends. As the environment changes, the model will need further tuning
in order to adapt, and as time goes on, you may decide to replace your model with a newer,
more capable model, necessitating tuning all over again. One nice thing is that fine-tuning
takes a lot less data and a lot fewer hardware resources than training, and can typically be
accomplished from a developer's laptop, depending on what type you choose.
If you're interested in learning how to fine-tune yourself, tools such as Unsloth (https://
unsloth.ai) make it easier and help you achieve fine-tuning and optimize for hardware
configurations that may not have many GPUs.
There are several types of fine-tuning as well, which we'll very briefly describe here.

Supervised fine-tuning
Good news! If you've been labeling and annotating your observability data per our
recommendations, that will help idx_94d0275b with the success of your fine-tuning should you choose the
supervised learning method. This method involves supplying a large amount of supplemental
data, all properly labeled and deduplicated, to the model. The data loaded into the model
needs to be clearly labeled so that the model knows not just what the sample data is, but also
what it means, such as text snippets and the sentiment classification, if you're doing sentiment
analysis. For AIOps, that might mean example alerts and metrics, the expected runbook to
correct an alert, and what should happen after the runbook is executed. Basically, it means as
many examples of data, tasks, and what success looks like as possible.
Few-shot learning
For few-shot learning, the data you'll supply is basically the same as with supervised learning,
but in a smaller volume. If you idx_ccdb33bf don't have very much data or very many examples, then you
give the few examples you do have while prompting the model, helping it to understand what
success would look like.
Transfer learning
Transfer learning is fine-tuning idx_abdbbea9 specifically for taking an LLM that has been trained on one
specific domain and providing it with further training data that allows it to use that skill for a
very niche application. An example is if you have a language model that's specifically trained
on a spoken language, and you adapt it to be a chatbot for a help desk.
Domain-specific fine-tuning
This is the fine-tuning where the model learns the specifics about the domain it needs to be
applied to. For example, documentation idx_1b5ac566 on AWS (or Kubernetes for our use cases) would be
supplied to the model to increase its domain-specific knowledge.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)
PEFT is a category of fine-tuning idx_540f0cf5 that modifies only a part of the data parameters. If the other
types of fine-tuning are adjustments to a building's facade, PEFT is just a new coat of paint.
Faster, cheaper, and with fewer hardware requirements, PEFT can be done without a GPU at
all. PEFT is a modification of the fewest parameters possible, which helps reduce risks and
prevent situations such as catastrophic forgetting. PEFT also requires the least amount of data
compared to other fine-tuning techniques.

Continuous learning
Continuous learning is an option instead of fine-tuning, or in conjunction with it. For systems
where there's just not any pre-existing data to speak of, you can have the model set to learn as
it runs in production. This idx_a4b3dfa2 means quick time to production use and no downtime for training.
However, it does come with higher risks for catastrophic forgetting and subsequent production
outages. For AIOps, despite the risk, continuous learning can be a valid option for use cases
where predictive maintenance and earlier detection of possible production incidents can be
valuable.
While continuous learning is riskier than fine-tuning, both do present the risk of catastrophic
forgetting. During your training processes, you can create model checkpoints (basically
snapshots in time), which you can restore from in the event of an otherwise recoverable error.
Breaking down your options
It's not enough to know idx_1484c71a what fine-tuning is. It's important to know how to decide which type
of fine-tuning is right for your organization. The amount of data you have to use for tuning, the
amount of time you want to invest, and the hardware available to you will all factor into this
decision. Prompt engineering and context engineering work together with fine-tuning, but can
stand alone, whereas fine-tuning does not prevent you from needing to leverage those

GPUs are expensive
Graphical processing units (GPUs) are in very high demand, making them more expensive to
purchase or rent. They also idx_483b5b1c use more electricity and generate more heat than other processors,
making idx_d2f9621a them costly to run and keep cool, even when you do have the hardware available.
In addition to token management, batch processing can also help keep your GPU costs lower.
Batch processing is the grouping of several similar tasks to be done together. If you're familiar
with batch processing in software already, this is just more of the same. Good candidates for
batch processing are AI-driven trend analysis jobs or pruning of retained logs to filter out noise.
Batches are also typically well distributed and likely scheduled so they'll be executed when
system utilization is otherwise lower.
GPUs are just processing units like central processing units (CPUs) are. Most of the same
techniques for lowering CPU idx_b7e092a4 utilization will transfer to GPUs. There are also ways to run AI
workloads that would usually need GPUs on CPUs. For this, another open source tool comes to
the rescue, vLLM (https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/).
vLLM is a specific Kubernetes implementation of AI inference. In vLLM, there's a mechanism
for offloading AI work from idx_5704e8b4 GPU and video random access memory (vRAM) to CPU and
dynamic random access memory (DRAM). CPUs and DRAM are less expensive, more
environmentally idx_f8580de3 friendly, and more readily available than their graphical counterparts,
allowing you to size the environment you need for AI inference in an expense-conscious way.
The larger your model, the idx_14a3d617 more vRAM is required to run it. Model size is determined in data
parameters, and DeepSeek-R1, which we've been using throughout the book, comes in several
sizes between 1.5B and 671B, where B stands for billions of parameters. We've largely been
using the 7B and 8B models, which can still require ~32 GB of VRAM to run well. Some of the
errors you saw in Chapter 2 were brute-forced into existence through the process of running
DeepSeek on hardware without sufficient VRAM available.
SLMs, which we've discussed a few times, have far fewer parameters, up to 10B as a rule. This
allowed them to tune faster than LLMs and allows them to run in a more resource- and cost-
efficient manner. SLMs use the same fundamental architecture as LLMs; however, they have
significantly less training data. It's fair to say that an SLM is purpose-built, whereas an LLM is
general-purpose.
An SLM may be less accurate or more prone to hallucination when prompted to solve tasks that
fall outside of the purpose for which they were built. You will see SLMs implemented in IoT
settings and on mobile devices where the hardware constraints are more significant than on

chunks.heading: Chapter 9 324
chunks.content:
large servers or in the cloud. The other notable drawback to an SLM over an LLM is that your
prompts need to be more precise and, therefore, lengthier. Breaking your SLM prompts down
into small, consumable chunks with a clear task list to act as checkpoints will help the SLM
325 No Future Without Challenges
maintain a more coherent context and a more focused and, therefore, accurate response. What
you save in hardware needs you pay for to some degree in token usage, making tuning more
critical for SLMs than for more robust models with vast knowledge bases.

Cost-benefit analysis
When approaching a project, start with a problem statement. What is it we seek to achieve
with our use of AIOps? The idx_74d12141 answer can't just be the use of AI; it must be something that has
tangible, measurable value.
There are other approaches, but cost-benefit is old enough to be well understood and versatile
enough to be useful in emerging fields such as cybersecurity. This is where those OKRs and
KPIs from Chapter 2 come in handy. Known goals and metrics already have values assigned, so
they do not require the same level of justification as novel factors. Showing why strongly
positive user sentiment should have a specific monetary value is enough effort by itself; there is
no need to re-evaluate why other business factors are important.
What may be financially expensive may also have benefits that outweigh that surface value.
It's important to assess that relationship to lend upfront clarity to decisions to build, buy, or
adopt new technologies and solutions. With these steps, you ensure that your desired project
has a well-defined scope and goals.
By assessing first, you determine at which point the numbers on the balance sheet start
working in your favor and can set yourself and your organization up for success and longevity.
There are many good templates for cost-benefit analysis, some of which are free. We chose to
follow this guide from Harvard (https://online.hbs.edu/blog/post/cost-benefit-
analysis), but while we present one format here, you can choose a different one if that helps.

What's different about security in an AI environment?
New technologies, new problems, right? Well, yes and no. Computing tends to follow certain
patterns; as such, those idx_7f6b5e94 patterns are easily repeatable even when technology is rapidly
changing. Best practices tend to look consistent whether you're securing computers in 2006 or
2026.
The most novel aspect of cybersecurity for AI systems is the model itself. It throws a bit of a
chaos variable into the mix, as there's never a 100% guarantee on what decisions it will make
or how it will understand data and input.
A model's knowledge is also frozen in time, unless augmented by systems such as RAG. If
you're using AI as a coding assistant, it also may not know about vulnerabilities and malware
in packages and may accidentally import something compromised because its training data
cut off while that was the latest version of the package.
Let's look at an imaginary scenario.
You're working on a new demo UI for a pitch. You decide to leverage a coding assistant whose
training data cuts off in 2024. You give it the correct prompts and tell it to follow best practices
and import specific versions of all dependencies, not just grab version tags such as latest.
Unfortunately, this leads to installing a version of a common package that was infected with
malware. If you deploy that code onto a production environment, or possibly even run it
locally, you could be exposing your organization to a security breach. Therefore, it's really
important to have security and vulnerability scanning locally and on production systems,
which we'll cover more shortly.
Injection attacks are also much easier with AI, since instead of writing code, a Markdown file
with instructions for an AI agent is the only thing that needs to be injected. For Claude and
other assistants, a marketplace of skills has been created. These skills augment the base skills
to serve specific purposes, and you can build custom skills or select one from their
